accuracy.evidence: Checked against AQA GCSE Physics 8463 section 4.6.1.2 ('frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second', unit hertz; period = 1 / frequency, T = 1/f) and the KS3 programme of study (frequencies of sound waves measured in hertz). Lab values checked in code and by hand: f = 4 Hz gives T = 0.25 s; the table rows 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 Hz give T = 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.2, 0.1 s and f × T = 1; T = 0.02 s gives 5 waves in the 0.1 s window and 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz (UK mains frequency); the 440 Hz target (A above middle C, ISO 16) is accepted for T = 2.25 ms (444 Hz) or 2.30 ms (435 Hz), within 10 Hz, and 1 ÷ 440 = 0.00227 s ≈ 2.3 ms; match pairs 0.5 s ↔ 2 Hz, 0.1 s ↔ 10 Hz, 20 ms = 0.02 s ↔ 50 Hz, 2 s ↔ 0.5 Hz. Parameterised items checked at range corners: p2 k, p3 1/f for f in {1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100} (exact to 2 dp), m4 always 1, m7 n ÷ 2n = 0.5.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented student errors on frequency and period (IOP Supporting Physics Teaching: waves; AQA examiner reports on T = 1/f questions): frequency and period taken as the same number (tags same/copy, m1, the 20 Hz and 2 Hz decoys in the match step); believing frequency and period rise together (step 2 prediction 'doubles', tags up/flat, p5, m8); reading 1 Hz as a length or height (step 1 prediction, tags len/amp, p1); using milliseconds in f = 1/T (the 0.05 Hz decoy with its own message, tag ms, m3); decimal slips (tag dec, m5 '0.5 s', tag pct for 0.25 vs 25); and multiplying instead of dividing (440 s and 50 s options, tag times).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghz is about the reciprocal link itself: a slider sets waves per second on a 1 s displacement-time strip with a dot at the end of every whole wave; a table fills as each frequency is tried so f × T = 1 is seen row by row; on a 0.1 s and a 10 ms axis the learner drags the end of the first wave (the period) and the 'waves in the window' count and f = 1 ÷ T update live; then periods in s and ms are matched to frequencies with decoys. flagwread reads λ and T off two static graphs, flagvfl works with v = fλ and flagwave wiggles a rope; none drags a period to set a frequency or tunes to a target. 6-shingle similarity is at most 2.5% (with flag_record.js) against every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each idea in the trace before the text states it: setting 4 Hz squeezes four waves into the 1 s strip and the bracket shrinks to 0.25 s; trying 1, 2, 4, 5 and 10 Hz shows the period bracket halving as the frequency doubles; dragging the period handle from 0.05 s to 0.02 s makes more waves fit the 0.1 s window (2 to 5), so 50 per second follows; tuning to 440 Hz shows a high note needs waves of only about 2.3 ms, and the feedback says which way to move ('shorter waves give a higher frequency'); a wrong match explains the slip (ms not converted, same number as the period).

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 1 Hz means 'each wave is 1 m long' or '1 m high' (the strip counts waves per second); if the frequency doubles the period 'doubles' or 'stays the same' (the table halves it); T = 0.02 s gives '0.02 Hz' or '2 Hz' (the window shows 5 waves in 0.1 s, so 50 Hz); a 440 Hz wave lasts '440 s' or '0.44 s' (tuning lands near 2.3 ms).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eleven distinct wrong-answer messages in hint(), each naming the slip: same (frequency and period are not the same number), pct (0.25 is a quarter, not 25), len (that is wavelength), amp (that is amplitude), ms (1 ÷ 20 used ms; convert to 0.02 s), copy (the frequency is not the period number), times (many waves each second means T is under 1 s), dec (1 ÷ 50 = 0.02, check 50 × 0.02 = 1), up (more waves each second means each is quicker), flat (T changes when f changes), kilo (0.44 s would be about 2 Hz). setT and pickF add live direction and conversion feedback in the lab steps.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes for the learner audience (kid and adult text within the readability limits). Ages 13-15 wording: one idea per sentence, every quantity named with its symbol and unit (frequency f in Hz, period T in s), reciprocal explained as 'f = 1 ÷ T and T = 1 ÷ f; multiply them and you get 1'. Lab readouts show the working in full (f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz).

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passes (no banned phrases, explanation overlap under 12% with every lesson). Kid paragraphs: frequency and hertz; period with the 4 Hz example; the reciprocal and doubling/halving; units and the 20 ms and 440 Hz examples. Adult paragraphs: spec statement and key words; named common mistakes; the f × T = 1 check and where frequency and period appear; what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: Before/after Show me screenshots of all six steps on iPhone 13 (390 px) and 360 px Android in light and dark, and desktop. First pass had the f-T table running into the slider label and '1 waves' wording; fixed by dropping the slider label in the table step, moving the table to sit between the axis labels and the slider, and singular/plural wording. Axis labels thin to every fifth tick on phones; the slider knob is 30 px with a 68 px tall grab band; the period handle accepts a drag anywhere within the trace height; match cards are at least 46 px tall; control buttons wrap below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: 'Lower the frequency by 0.5 hertz' / 'Raise…', 'Set 4 hertz' for each table row, 'Make the period a little shorter' / 'much longer', 'Period 20 ms' then 'Frequency 50 Hz'; challenge answers are 'Answer: …' buttons. voice() updates the canvas aria-label and the visible narration after every action (e.g. 'T = 0.02 s, so f = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz'). walk.cjs: desktop and iPhone 13 complete all 5 tasks with Show me, the challenge shows, axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes, no console errors. Canvas text is navy on pale tags in both themes; the trace switches to a lighter blue in the dark theme.
